title: HTTP / HTTPS
tagline: The protocol every API call, page load and webhook travels on.
overview: Every endpoint you build speaks HTTP, and every production deployment speaks HTTPS. Understanding the protocol makes debugging dramatically faster: most "the API is broken" problems are a header, a status code, a cookie attribute, a certificate or a proxy setting.
objectives: Read and write raw HTTP requests and responses.
Use status codes, cookies and sessions correctly.
Explain how TLS secures HTTPS and how certificates are verified.
notes: Debug with `curl -v` and the browser's Network tab.
Status codes are part of your API contract.

explain: TLS handshake at a high level
build: A tiny HTTP server with Python's http.server to inspect raw requests

tasks.title: Raw HTTP
steps: Run `python -m http.server 8000` and request it with `curl -v`.
Use `nc` (netcat) to type a raw `GET / HTTP/1.1` request with a Host header.
Compare headers sent by curl and by your browser (DevTools → Network).

tasks.title: Cookie lab
steps: Log into a local Django admin.
Inspect the sessionid cookie attributes in DevTools.
Delete the session row in the database and reload: you're logged out.

lessons.title: Client/server, requests, responses, headers and body
lessons.summary: The anatomy of an HTTP message and how clients and servers exchange them.
lessons.simple: HTTP is the request–response protocol of the web. A **client** (browser, mobile app, `curl`, another service) sends a **request**; a **server** returns a **response**. Both are text-structured messages with a start line, **headers**, and an optional **body**.
lessons.technical:
A request has:
- **Request line**: method, path, version — `GET /api/orders?page=2 HTTP/1.1`
- **Headers**: `Host: api.example.com` (required in 1.1), `Accept: application/json`, `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `User-Agent`, `Cookie`.
- **Body** (for POST/PUT/PATCH): e.g. JSON, with `Content-Type: application/json` and `Content-Length`.

A response has:
- **Status line**: `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`
- **Headers**: `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `Location`, CORS headers like `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
- **Body**: the representation.

HTTP itself is **stateless**: every request stands alone. State (logins, carts) is layered on with cookies or tokens.

Methods: GET (read), POST (create/act), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE, HEAD (headers only), OPTIONS (capabilities; used by CORS preflight).

`curl -v` shows the full exchange and is the best HTTP debugging tool you have.
lessons.analogy: An HTTP request is a letter: the envelope has the address and method of delivery (request line), the stamps and notes are headers, and the letter inside is the body. The reply comes back with a status stamped on the front.

example.code:
$ curl -v -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/orders \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJ..." \
    -d '{"product_id": 7, "qty": 2}'
> POST /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.example.com
> Content-Type: application/json
> Content-Length: 27
>
< HTTP/1.1 201 Created
< Content-Type: application/json
< Location: /v1/orders/981
<
{"id": 981, "status": "new"}
example.explain: Lines starting with `>` were sent; `<` were received. You can see method, path, headers, body, status and the Location of the new resource.

terms: Each request independent of previous ones.
remember: Request = line + headers + body; response = status + headers + body.
Content-Type tells the receiver how to parse the body.
mistakes: Putting sensitive data in query strings (logged everywhere).
interview: Walk through the parts of an HTTP request.
practice: Can you use: send a JSON POST with curl and read the response headers?
Can you debug: a 415 Unsupported Media Type response.

lessons.title: Status codes, cookies and sessions
lessons.summary: Status code classes, how cookies work, and how sessions add state to HTTP.
lessons.simple: **Status codes** summarize the result in three digits. **Cookies** are small values the server asks the browser to store and send back. **Sessions** use a cookie with an ID to remember a user across requests.
lessons.technical:
Status classes: **1xx** informational, **2xx** success (200, 201, 204), **3xx** redirection (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified for caching), **4xx** client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 405, 409, 429), **5xx** server error (500, 502, 503, 504).

**Cookies**: the server sends `Set-Cookie: sessionid=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=1209600`. The browser stores it and sends `Cookie: sessionid=abc123` with matching requests.
- `HttpOnly`: JavaScript can't read it (limits XSS token theft).
- `Secure`: only sent over HTTPS.
- `SameSite=Lax/Strict/None`: controls cross-site sending; key defense against CSRF.
- `Domain`, `Path`, `Expires/Max-Age` scope it.

**Sessions**: after login the server creates a session record (in DB/Redis) and sends only a random ID in a cookie. Each request, it looks the ID up to find the user. Logout deletes the record — instant revocation. Contrast with JWTs, which carry claims themselves and are hard to revoke before expiry.

Because browsers send cookies automatically, cookie-based auth needs **CSRF protection** (tokens + SameSite) for state-changing requests.
lessons.analogy: A session cookie is a coat-check ticket. The ticket itself is worthless; the cloakroom (server) keeps your coat (session data) and matches the number. Lose the ticket or the cloakroom throws away the coat, and you're logged out.

example.code:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=ana&password=********

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /dashboard
Set-Cookie: sessionid=k3j9x1...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/

GET /dashboard HTTP/1.1
Cookie: sessionid=k3j9x1...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
example.explain: Login sets a session cookie and redirects. The browser automatically attaches the cookie to the next request, which is how the server knows it's Ana.

terms: Response telling the client to go to Location.
Response header instructing the browser to store a cookie.
Server-side state keyed by an ID in a cookie.
remember: Session = random ID in cookie + data on server.
Cookies are auto-sent → protect against CSRF.
mistakes: Storing user data (like role) in a plain cookie the client can edit.
Auth cookies without Secure on HTTPS sites.
interview: How does a session-based login work?
What do HttpOnly and SameSite protect against?
practice: Can you explain: session cookies vs JWT for a web app?
Can you debug: users get logged out on every request (cookie domain/Secure on HTTP).

lessons.title: HTTPS, TLS basics and certificates
lessons.summary: How HTTPS keeps traffic private and proves server identity.
lessons.simple: **HTTPS** is HTTP sent inside a **TLS** connection. TLS **encrypts** traffic (no eavesdropping), protects **integrity** (no tampering), and **authenticates** the server with a certificate (you're talking to the real site).
lessons.technical:
Simplified TLS 1.3 handshake:
1. Client sends **ClientHello**: supported versions/ciphers and a key share; SNI names the hostname.
2. Server replies with its key share and its **certificate**, plus a signature proving it holds the private key.
3. Both derive the same **symmetric session keys** (via ephemeral Diffie–Hellman). Asymmetric crypto is used to authenticate and agree keys; fast symmetric crypto (AES-GCM, ChaCha20) encrypts the data.

**Certificates** (X.509) bind a domain name to a public key, signed by a **Certificate Authority (CA)**. The browser verifies the chain: site cert → intermediate → trusted root in the OS/browser store, and checks the hostname matches and the cert hasn't expired.

Practicalities:
- **Let's Encrypt** issues free 90-day certificates; automate renewal (certbot, Caddy, or your load balancer/CDN).
- TLS is often **terminated** at a reverse proxy (nginx, a load balancer); traffic behind it may be plain HTTP inside a private network. Django then needs `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` to know the original request was HTTPS.
- Redirect HTTP → HTTPS and send **HSTS** (`Strict-Transport-Security`) so browsers refuse plain HTTP next time.

HTTPS hides paths, headers and bodies, but not the IP address or (usually) the hostname via SNI/DNS.
lessons.analogy: A certificate is a passport: issued by a trusted government (CA), it ties a name (domain) to a face (public key). TLS is then speaking in a private code that only you and the verified passport holder agreed on.

example.code:
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
subject=CN = example.com
issuer=C = US, O = DigiCert Inc, CN = DigiCert Global G2 TLS RSA SHA256 2020 CA1
notBefore=Jan 13 00:00:00 2024 GMT
notAfter=Feb 13 23:59:59 2025 GMT

$ curl -I https://example.com | grep -i strict
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000
example.explain: You can inspect who a certificate was issued to, which CA signed it, and when it expires — the first checks when browsers show certificate errors.

terms: Protocol providing encryption, integrity and authentication.
Signed binding of a domain to a public key.
Decrypting at a proxy before forwarding.
Header forcing HTTPS on future visits.
remember: Asymmetric keys for the handshake, symmetric keys for data.
mistakes: Disabling certificate verification (`verify=False`) in production code.
Mixed content: HTTPS pages loading HTTP scripts.
interview: What does a certificate prove, and who vouches for it?
Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
practice: Can you use: inspect a site's certificate chain and expiry with openssl?
Can you debug: Django builds http:// URLs behind an HTTPS load balancer.

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
lessons.summary: How HTTP versions differ in connections, multiplexing and transport.
lessons.simple: The meaning of HTTP (methods, headers, status codes) stays the same across versions. What changes is how messages travel: **HTTP/1.1** is text over TCP, **HTTP/2** is binary and multiplexed over TCP, **HTTP/3** runs over **QUIC** on UDP.
lessons.technical:
**HTTP/1.1** (1997): persistent keep-alive connections, but one request at a time per connection; a slow response blocks the ones behind it (**head-of-line blocking** at the HTTP layer). Browsers open ~6 connections per host to compensate. Headers are repetitive plain text.

**HTTP/2** (2015): binary framing, **multiplexing** many concurrent streams over a single TCP connection, **HPACK** header compression, stream prioritization. Almost always over TLS in practice. It removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking — but one lost TCP packet still stalls **all** streams, because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order.

**HTTP/3** (2022): HTTP over **QUIC**, a transport on **UDP** with built-in TLS 1.3. Streams are independent at the transport level, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream. Faster connection setup (fewer round trips, 0-RTT resumption) and **connection migration** (survives switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data, thanks to connection IDs instead of IP/port tuples).

For backend engineers: your Django app usually speaks HTTP/1.1 to a reverse proxy/CDN, which speaks HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to clients. gRPC is built on HTTP/2.
lessons.analogy: HTTP/1.1 is a single-lane road: one slow truck blocks everyone. HTTP/2 is many lanes painted on one road, but a pothole (lost packet) still closes the whole road. HTTP/3 gives each lane its own road surface.

example.code:
$ curl -sI --http2 https://www.google.com | head -1
HTTP/2 200
$ curl -sI --http3 https://www.cloudflare.com | head -1     # needs curl built with HTTP/3
HTTP/3 200
$ curl -sI --http1.1 https://example.com | head -1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
example.explain: Same resource, same semantics, different wire protocols negotiated with the server (via TLS ALPN, and Alt-Svc for HTTP/3).

terms: A delayed item blocks the ones queued behind it.
Many streams interleaved over one connection.
Header compression for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
UDP-based transport with built-in TLS and independent streams.
TLS extension negotiating the HTTP version.
remember: Semantics are the same; transport differs.
HTTP/2 multiplexes over one TCP connection.
HTTP/3 = QUIC over UDP; fixes TCP-level head-of-line blocking.
mistakes: Thinking HTTP/2 changes your REST design.
Believing HTTP/3 means 'unreliable UDP' — QUIC adds reliability itself.
Domain sharding and sprite hacks kept from HTTP/1.1 days.
interview: What problem does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve, and what does it leave unsolved?
practice: Can you explain: head-of-line blocking at HTTP vs TCP level?
Can you use: check which HTTP version a site negotiates with curl.
